definition: Arena (formerly LMArena and Chatbot Arena) is a public, web-based platform that evaluates large language models (LLMs).
details: Users enter prompts for two anonymous models to respond to and vote on the model that gave the better response, after which the models' identities are revealed. Users can also choose models to test themselves via the "Direct" selection. Companies which have supplied the company with their large language models include OpenAI, Google DeepMind, and Anthropic. The website has been used for preview releases of upcoming models. Chinese company DeepSeek tested its prototype models in the Arena months before its R1 model gained attention in Western media. Other notable pre-release models include OpenAI's GPT-5 under the codename "summit" and Google DeepMind's Gemini 2.5 Flash Image (an image-generation and editing model) under the codename "Nano Banana". Research has identified specific limitations in Arena's methodology.

explainer.lead: Arena is a public website for comparing large language models through side-by-side tests. People judge two initially anonymous answers, making it a practical way to see which models users prefer and to try some models before their public release.

tiers.eli5: Imagine asking two hidden contestants the same question and picking the answer you like better. Arena does this with AI models: you vote, and then it tells you which models wrote the answers. You can also pick particular models yourself using Direct selection.
tiers.practitioner: Use Arena to compare model responses to a prompt without knowing their identities until after voting, or select models directly for a controlled test. It can provide a quick qualitative check and expose early model builds, but preference votes should not substitute for task-specific evaluation, and research has identified limitations in its methodology.
tiers.paperLevel: Arena is a web-based comparative evaluation platform: a prompt is issued to two models whose identities are initially concealed, and a user preference is recorded before those identities are disclosed. Direct selection permits user-chosen model comparisons. Methodological limitations have been identified, so the resulting preferences are not a comprehensive measure of model capability.

explainer.example: You ask two anonymous models to explain why the sky is blue. You prefer Response B because it is clearer, cast your vote, and only then see which models produced Responses A and B.

explainer.intuition: A blind taste test is a useful analogy: compare two answers on their merits first, then learn which model produced each one. Arena turns those human choices into public evidence about which responses people prefer.
howItWorks: A user enters a prompt for two anonymous models.
Both models generate responses, shown side by side.
The user votes for the better response.
Arena reveals the models' identities after the vote.
Alternatively, Direct selection lets the user choose models to test.
explainer.whyItMatters: Arena gives researchers, developers, and curious users a shared place to compare models using ordinary prompts and human judgments. Its preview appearances also offer early glimpses of models that have not yet been publicly released.
misconceptions: The models are anonymous only until the user votes; their identities are then revealed.
Users are not always given a random pairing: Direct selection lets them choose models.
A preference between two answers is not a complete assessment of either model.
